questions.title: What will be Donald Trump's net approval on December 31, 2026?
questions.background:
US President Donald Trump's net approval rating has long hovered between -10 and -20, with him holding an unprecedentedly [stable approval rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_on_the_first_Trump_presidency) during his first term. 

During Trump's second term, his approval has moved more substantially, starting with a positive approval rating, before dropping into a negative rating, reaching the high teens as of December 2025.
questions.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as Donald Trump's net approval rating on December 31, 2026, according to data from the [Silver Bulletin](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin).
questions.fine_print: If data for December 31, 2026 are not published by the Silver Bulletin, this question will resolve as Trump's net approval on the latest available day in December. If Silver Bulletin ceases to publish Trump's approval rating, this question will be **annulled**.

questions.title: Will any of Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, and/or Germany leave the EU before 2027?
questions.background:
Anti-European sentiment is running strong in the EU and it may grow stronger – strong enough to destroy it, maybe? The UK voted for Brexit and political pundits are already discussing [Nexit](http://www.express.co.uk/news/world/717904/Nexit-Dutch-turn-right-euroscepticism-Geert-Wilders-Mark-Rutte), [Frexit](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2016/jun/27/frexit-nexit-or-oexit-who-will-be-next-to-leave-the-eu) and [Quitaly](https://www.theguardian.com/business/economics-blog/2016/jul/26/italy-economy-banks-loans-crisis-europe).

Some commentators argue that Brexit is already the end of the EU as we know it, some would say that Brexit may be fine but if any other country was to leave would spell the end of the union. We choose an even stricter criterion by requiring then one of the [6 original founders of the ECSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Six) leave the union to decree the end of the EU as we know it.
questions.resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as **Yes** if, before January 1, 2027, one or more of Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, and/or Germany triggers Article 50 of the Treaty of Lisbon by notifying the European Council of its intention to leave the union.

It also resolves as positive if by the same deadline the entity called European Union  has dissolved completely or dissolved to create a new politico-economic union of some European nations under a different name

questions.title: Will the sitting U.S. president’s net worth reach ≥4x its value before they became president at any point in the following years? (2025-2026)
questions.background: [<u>For Donald Trump, Forbes estimated his net worth at \$2.6 billion on January 12, 2024</u>](https://web.archive.org/web/20240112150444/https://www.forbes.com/profile/donald-trump/). [<u>The Forbes 400 estimates</u>](https://www.forbes.com/forbes-400/) of Trump’s net worth (released each fall) were \$4.3 billion in 2024 and \$7.3 billion in 2025. There is no credible record of a U.S. president’s personal wealth quadrupling during their presidency in history, but [Trump’s holdings in Trump Media & Technology Group](https://www.forbes.com/sites/danalexander/article/the-definitive-networth-of-donaldtrump/) (DJT) could provide a vehicle for unprecedented wealth accumulation.
questions.resolution_criteria: Each subquestion will resolve as **Yes** if, at any point in the corresponding two-year period, the sitting president’s net worth equals or exceeds 4 times its earliest value in the year before they take office.
questions.fine_print:
* Each subquestion will use the earliest archived estimate of the president's net worth from the year before they took office. If a president served for two, non-consecutive terms, the year before they assumed office for a second time will be used.
* The primary source to resolve each subquestion will be Forbes. Net worth is calculated using Forbes’ real time net worth calculator. E.g, as reported by Forbes, Trump’s net worth was[ <u>\$2.6 billion</u>](https://web.archive.org/web/20240112150444/https://www.forbes.com/profile/donald-trump/) on January 12, 2024. Since Forbes does not provide historical data, the Internet Archive’s[ <u>Wayback Machine</u>](https://web.archive.org/) will be used to determine if/when a president crosses or equals the corresponding threshold.
* If data from Forbes are not available, we will instead use estimates from the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. If neither are available or lack an updated estimate for the relevant president, the subquestion will resolve according to required financial disclosures filed by candidates for and holders of federal office and other credible sources.

questions.title: How many of these 15 top US executive branch officials will be out before 2027?
questions.background:
Donald Trump's first term was characterized by a historic amount of turnover. According to the [Brookings Institution](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/tracking-turnover-in-the-trump-administration/), the occupants of senior level positions got fired, quit, or otherwise left their positions in the following numbers:

| President        | N      | Year 1  | Year 2  | Year 3  | Year 4 | Total turnover |
| ---------------- | ------ | ------- | ------- | ------- | ------ | -------------- |
| Ronald Reagan    | 60     | 17%     | 40%     | 13%     | 8%     | 78%            |
| George H.W. Bush | 57     | 7%      | 18%     | 32%     | 9%     | 66%            |
| Bill Clinton     | 70     | 11%     | 27%     | 20%     | 16%    | 74%            |
| George W. Bush   | 63     | 6%      | 27%     | 25%     | 5%     | 63%            |
| Barack Obama     | 53     | 9%      | 15%     | 43%     | 4%     | 71%            |
| **Donald Trump** | **65** | **35%** | **31%** | **17%** | **9%** | **92%**        |

Additionally, several roles under Trump had what Brookings calls "serial turnover," such as four National Security Advisors in the four years, four White House Chiefs of Staff and four Press Secretaries.

At the time of this question's writing, none of the listed roles had turned over. However, there have been calls for many to resign or be fired:

* In December 2025 there were [calls](https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/5634559-republicans-hegseth-leadership-pentagon/) for Pete Hegseth to resign over the killing of four crew members of an alleged drug smuggling boat. 
* Calls for Pam Bondi to resign, which [gained](https://www.newsweek.com/petition-pam-bondi-signatures-resign-2098711) [steam](https://www.cnn.com/2025/07/07/politics/bondi-epstein-files-client-list-suicide-memo) over her handling of files related to convicted child molester Jeffrey Epstein. Dan Bongino [nearly resigned](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/dan-bongino-weighs-resigning-fbi-heated-confrontation-pam-bondi-epstei-rcna218388) over the controversy in July.
* Scrutiny over Kash Patel's handling of FBI resources, [such as](https://www.ms.now/news/kash-patel-girlfriend-fbi-detail-wilkins-ride-home) having FBI agents drive one of his girlfriend's inebriated friends home after a night of drinking.
questions.resolution_criteria:
This question resolves as the number of the following 15 officials who leave their position, formally announce they will leave their position, or whose agency announces that they have left or will leave their position, before January 1, 2027:

| Role                                                           | Incumbent             |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Secretary of State and National Security Advisor               | Marco Rubio           |
| Secretary of the Treasury                                      | Scott Bessent         |
| Secretary of Defense                                           | Pete Hegseth          |
| Attorney General                                               | Pam Bondi             |
| Secretary of Health & Human Services                           | Robert F. Kennedy Jr. |
| Secretary of Commerce                                          | Howard Lutnick        |
| Secretary of Homeland Security                                 | Kristi Noem           |
| Director of National Intelligence                              | Tulsi Gabbard         |
| Director of the Central Intelligence Agency                    | John Ratcliffe        |
| OMB Director                                                   | Russell Vought        |
| White House Chief of Staff                                     | Susie Wiles           |
| DOJ (FBI) Director                                             | Kash Patel            |
| Border Czar                                                    | Tom Homan             |
| Senior Counselor for Trade/Manufacturing                       | Peter Navarro         |
| Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy and Homeland Security Advisor | Stephen Miller        |
questions.fine_print: Any person in more than one listed role at the opening of this question must leave both roles in order to count.

questions.title: When will martial law be lifted in at least 3/4 of Ukraine?
questions.background:
[Martial law](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law_in_Ukraine) was declared in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, in response to the Russian invasion.

Martial law was originally declared for 30 days. It has since been prolonged three times: by 30, 30, and 90 days respectively. Therefore, it would end on August 25, 2022 if not prolonged again or canceled.

The decision to prolong martial law is made by the security council and the president and is subject to approval by the parliament.

Martial law can be also declared in some of the regions as opposed to the whole country, like it was [in 2018](https://edition.cnn.com/2018/11/26/europe/ukraine-russia-kerch-strait-intl/index.html).
questions.resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the earliest date after May 1, 2022 when at least 3/4 of Ukraine's Oblasts (top-level administrative districts as defined by the Ukrainian government; currently the 24 oblasts and Crimea) do not have martial law declared in the entire territory by the Ukrainian government.  Any regions of Ukraine partially or fully [occupied by another state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupied_territories_of_Ukraine) will be excluded.

If this does not occur by May 29, 2027, the question will resolve as **>May 28, 2027**. If the present-day Ukrainian government ceases to exist and/or no longer controls any territory recognized as Ukrainian as of January 1, 2022, this question will resolve as **Ambiguous**

questions.title: What will the average new forecasters per day be on this question before this question closes?
questions.background: This question helps encourage bots to be aware of the open/close date of a question. Bots should assume a question has not yet been resolved by the time a question opens.
questions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves to the number of forecasters listed in the Metaculus UI on the close date for this question divided by the number of days this question is open. The question will round to the nearest hundredth.

questions.title: What will the average interest rate on the US federal government's total debt be at the end of these fiscal years? (FY 2028 (ending Sep 30, 2028))
questions.background:
As of the end of FY 2024, the US government had \$35.46 trillion in debt. It made over \$1.1 trillion in interest payments, one of the highest spending items for the year: 

| Name                                                 | Obligated Amount        | Percent of Total |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------------- |
| Medicare                                             | \$1,582,650,103,296     | 16.34%           |
| Social Security                                      | \$1,541,027,236,655     | 15.91%           |
| National Defense                                     | \$1,358,253,371,219     | 14.03%           |
| **Net Interest on national debt**                    | **\$1,149,557,674,231** | **11.87%**       |
| Health                                               | \$1,098,419,579,301     | 11.34%           |
| Income Security                                      | \$717,980,743,457       | 7.41%            |
| General Government                                   | \$477,396,451,071       | 4.93%            |
| Veterans Benefits and Services                       | \$368,773,705,656       | 3.81%            |
| Education, Training, Employment, and Social Services | \$270,345,605,294       | 2.79%            |
| Transportation                                       | \$176,918,553,558       | 1.83%            |

([source](https://www.usaspending.gov/explorer/budget_function))

Notably, The average interest rate on the US national debt at year-end was 3.32%. Thirty years ago, in 1995, the average interest paid on US government securities [was](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/rptcongress/ann95.pdf) 6.34%. Should interest on US government debt rise back to that level, the government in 2024 numbers would be making about \$2.25 trillion in interest payments, making it by far the largest spending item, larger than the current largest items of Social Security (\$1.5 trillion), Medicare (\$1.6 trillion), and national defense (\$1.4 trillion). Should interest paid rise to 10%, which were levels reached [in 1982](https://www.cbpp.org/research/federal-budget/deficits-debt-and-interest), interest on the national debt would be \$3.5 trillion, which would be 71% of the 4.92 trillion in revenue the government collected in 2024.

In the past decade, the history of the US government's debt, end-of-year interest rate, and interest obligation for the next year are as follows:

| FY   | Debt (USD trillions) | Avg Interest Rate (EoY) | Next-Year Interest Obligation (USD trillions) |
| ---- | -------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| 2015 | 24.07                | 2.35%                   | 0.57                                          |
| 2016 | 25.59                | 2.23%                   | 0.57                                          |
| 2017 | 25.89                | 2.28%                   | 0.59                                          |
| 2018 | 26.90                | 2.49%                   | 0.67                                          |
| 2019 | 27.93                | 2.49%                   | 0.70                                          |
| 2020 | 32.67                | 1.77%                   | 0.58                                          |
| 2021 | 32.71                | 1.61%                   | 0.53                                          |
| 2022 | 32.89                | 2.07%                   | 0.68                                          |
| 2023 | 34.13                | 2.97%                   | 1.01                                          |
| 2024 | 35.46                | 3.32%                   | 1.18                                          |

A notable forecast about the trajectory of the interest rate on the national debt is from the Congressional Budget Office [Budget and Economic Outlook: 2024 to 2034](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/59946#_idTextAnchor045), which says:

> Average interest rates on federal debt rise in CBO’s projections as debt matures and is refinanced. In 2025, the average interest rate on debt held by the public is projected to be 3.4 percent, 0.1 percentage point higher than it was in 2024 and 0.7 percentage points higher than it was in 2023. That rate generally remains steady thereafter, declining slightly to 3.3 percent from 2027 through 2030 before increasing again to 3.5 percent in the final years of the projection period. Changes in the average interest rate stem from interest rates on Treasury securities, the rate of inflation applicable to Treasury inflation-protected securities, and the maturity structure of outstanding securities. (For a discussion of the factors responsible for changes in interest rates and inflation, see [Chapter 2](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/59946#_idTextAnchor070).)
questions.resolution_criteria: These subquestions resolve as the average interest rate amount, expressed as a percent, paid by the United States government on its total interest-bearing debt [according to the US Treasury](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/interest-expense-avg-interest-rates/) at the end of each respective fiscal year.

questions.title: What will net outlays by the US government be in millions of dollars in FY 2028?
questions.background:
Net outlays are the actual cash paid out by the US federal government in a given year, the equivalent of cash accounting. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) [defines](https://budgetcounsel.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/page-77-78.pdf) outlays as:

> The issuance of checks, disbursement of cash, or electronic transfer of funds made to liquidate a federal obligation. Outlays also occur when interest on the Treasury debt held by the public accrues and when the government issues bonds, notes, debentures, monetary credits, or other cash-equivalent instruments in order to liquidate obligations. Also, under credit reform, the credit subsidy cost is recorded as an outlay when a direct or guaranteed loan is disbursed. An outlay is not recorded for repayment of debt principal, disbursements to the public by federal credit programs for direct loan obligations and loan guarantee commitments made in fiscal year 1992 or later, disbursements from deposit funds, and refunds of receipts that result from overpayments. Outlays during a fiscal year may be for payment of obligations incurred in prior years (prior-year obligations) or in the same year. Outlays, therefore, flow in part from unexpended balances of prior-year budgetary resources and in part from budgetary resources provided for the year in which the money is spent.

In 2024, federal government outlays were \$6.75 trillion and made up 23% of the US's Gross Domestic Product (GDP). On January 20, 2025, Donald J. Trump was inaugurated as the 47th US President, and that same day he [established](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/establishing-and-implementing-the-presidents-department-of-government-efficiency/) the Department of Governmental Efficiencey (DOGE), headed by Elon Musk. Musk has [stated a goal](https://www.yahoo.com/news/elon-musk-and-doge-promised-up-to-2-trillion-in-government-savings-how-much-have-they-actually-saved-so-far-201718142.html) of saving up to \$2 trillion annual expenditures by 2026. At the time of this question, the [DOGE website](https://doge.gov/savings) has tallied \$130 billion in savings.

In FY 2024, federal budget allocations [were](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/breaking-down-the-u-s-governments-2024-fiscal-year/) as follows:

| Function                      | Amount      |
| ----------------------------- | ----------- |
| Social Security               | \$1,461     |
| Health                        | \$912       |
| Net Interest                  | \$882       |
| Medicare                      | \$874       |
| National Defense              | \$874       |
| Income Security               | \$671       |
| Veterans' Benefits & Services | \$325       |
| Education                     | \$305       |
| Transportation                | \$137       |
| Other                         | \$311       |
| **Total Outlays**             | **\$6,752** |

In addition to the efforts of DOGE to cut outlays, the US Congress, of which both Houses are under Republican control at the time of this question, is working on the next budget under Senate reconciliation rules. Please see the [2025 Reconciliation Tracker](https://www.crfb.org/blogs/2025-reconciliation-tracker) by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. See also from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania: [The FY2025 House Budget reconciliation and Trump Administration Tax Proposals: Budgetary, Economic, and Distributional Effects](https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/issues/2025/2/27/fy2025-house-budget-reconciliation-and-trump-tax-proposals-effects)
questions.resolution_criteria: This question resolves as the amount of [Federal Net Outlays](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYONET) in the United States in millions of dollars in Fiscal Year 2028, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED).
questions.fine_print:
This question will resolve as the number shown by FRED, which represents millions of USD. For example, in 2024, this question would have resolved as **6,751,552**, as the net outlays were \$6,751,552,000,000. Therefore, when viewing the resolution source, please ensure (via the Edit Graph button) that:

* *Units* are set to **Millions of Dollars**.
* *Frequency* is set to Annual, Fiscal Year.

This question resolves based upon the first update by FRED incorporating federal net outlays for FY 2028. Further revisions after this question has been resolved will not be considered.

questions.title: Which party's nominee will win the 2028 US presidential election?
questions.background:
American voters elect their president every four years. The 2028 presidential election will be open, with President Donald J. Trump term limited (in October 2025 [saying](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-acknowledges-he-cant-run-for-a-third-term-its-too-bad/#) it's "pretty clear" he is not allowed to run for a third term and that the idea of him running for vice president would be "too cute").

Following the chaos of the 2020 election, which led to fake electors being sent to Washington, D.C. and formal [objections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_States_Electoral_College_vote_count#Announcements_of_planned_Electoral_College_vote_count_objections) by certain Republican members of Congress to the counting of Electoral College votes, Congress in 2022 [passed](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/electoral-count-reform-act-congress-january-6/) the bipartisan Electoral Count Reform Act. It set a much higher threshold for formal objections, requiring one-fifth of members of each chamber of Congress to sign any objection (previously the requirement was just one in each chamber). Additionally, Congress now considers electors sent by state governments to be conclusive and that the federal courts rather than Congress are the final deciders of any questions about apportionment of electors.

In late summer 2028, the two parties are expected to hold their nominating conventions. Please see:

* [Who will be the 2028 Democratic nominee for President of the United States?](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/37322/who-will-be-the-2028-democratic-nominee-for-president-of-the-united-states/)
* [Who will be the 2028 Republican nominee for President of the United States?](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/37321/who-will-be-the-2028-republican-nominee-for-president-of-the-united-states/)
questions.resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the party whose candidate wins the [2028 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_United_States_presidential_election).

If the winner of the 2028 US presidential election does not represent either party or if the election is not conducted in 2028, then this question will resolve as **Other**.
questions.fine_print:
Under the US Constitution, the winner of the presidential election is the candidate who receives the most votes in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_College_\(United_States\)), which means a simple majority (270) of the 538 electors. This question will resolve once a candidate has secured at least 270 Electoral College votes according to [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) including media projections. In case of any material uncertainty, however, such as occurred following the [2020 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attempts_to_overturn_the_2020_United_States_presidential_election), Metaculus may delay resolution until the date Congress certifies the votes.

If no candidate secures 270 votes (such as in a tie), the question will resolve when the US House of Representatives [elects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingent_election) the President.
